text: The Eisberg, and its glacier, catching the last of the sun. Somewhere under all that ice there's a hangar, twelve black aircraft, and a very pleased Colonel.
A red cable car crawling up to a station on the glacier. PRIVATE, says the sign. Bank staff only. Banks in Switzerland keep their vaults inside mountains. Very secure. Very cold.
A rack of skis in every colour. The last time I skied I was twelve, and I went through a fence.
A steel door with a card slot. GLETSCHERBAHN: PRIVATE. Brunner goes up there. I need whatever Brunner opens it with.
The card will open the cable car, and the vault. But a Swiss vault will want a number too. Brunner won't have written it down. Brunner is the sort who hides it in plain sight.
Not yet. That clock is still ticking in the shop, and at noon it opens Vasko's hangar.
Sepp, the head of the ski school: seventy years old, the colour of a saddle, and not an ounce of fat on him. He has been skiing since before skis.
Herr Brunner of Zürich, in a white ski suit that has never touched snow. Around his neck, on a chain, a steel card. He keeps patting it, like a man checking his heart is still there.
Something steel, glinting in the snowdrift where Brunner landed.
BANK BRUNNER & CIE, GLETSCHERTRESOR. The glacier vault. Herr Brunner dropped his heart in the snow.
I have paid for a private lesson! Four hundred francs! Where is my instructor?
Herr Brunner, my instructor Klaus has broken his leg. Twice. On the same day. I am looking for another.
Then find one! I have a meeting on the glacier tomorrow, and I will not arrive on my bottom.
Brunner. Herr Brunner of Zürich: the banker from Istanbul, and from the ball in Venice. The money for Nightglass goes through his bank, and his bank's vault is up on that glacier.
Hot chocolate for two hours, he says. You are the worst instructor I ever had, Johann. Also the best. He paid double.
Go on, Johann! Herr Brunner is waiting. Knees bent, and do not let him near the church.
Grüezi. You look like a man who needs a job. Can you ski?
Like a champion.
Everybody says that. Klaus said that. Now Klaus is in two plasters.
I've seen it on television.
Good! That is more than Herr Brunner. He thinks skis are for standing on in the bar.
Honestly? Not really.
An honest man! In Grindelhorn! You are hired. Herr Brunner does not need a good skier. He needs a patient one.
Here. The red jacket. Now you are Johann, of the Skischule Sepp. Smile, and say "Knees!" a lot.
Johann, ski instructor. Knees!
Are you the instructor? No? Then please step aside. You are standing in my light, and I am paying for the light.
Herr Brunner. Johann, from the Skischule Sepp. Shall we begin?
At last. I must be able to stop by tomorrow. Stopping is the only thing a banker needs to know.
Bend your knees.
They are bent. They have been bent since 1954.
Point the tips together, like a slice of pizza.
I am Swiss. I do not know what a pizza is. I know what a fondue is.
Lean forward, and trust the mountain.
I trust nothing. I am a banker.
Now push off. Gently.
It is moving! Why is it moving? How do I stop? Johann, how do I stop?
plough
Snowplough!
fall
Fall over!
Aim for something soft!
Mmmf. Mmmmmf. I have stopped.
That was the most expensive lesson of my life, and I have been to Monte Carlo. I shall have a hot chocolate. For two hours. Put it on my account.
He crawled out of the snowdrift and went straight to the hotel. He didn't notice what he left behind in it.
Grüezi! Welcome to Zimmerli Uhren: cuckoo clocks since 1882. And please, the goose stays by the door. The goose and the cuckoos, they will not be friends.
Dozens of cuckoo clocks, all ticking, all slightly out of time with each other. On the hour it must sound like an aviary being attacked.
A clock with BRUNNER painted underneath. Stopped at a quarter to twelve, and the second hand at thirty. Eleven, forty-five, thirty.
Eleven, forty-five, thirty. One, one, four, five, three, nought. A banker who never lets anyone change the time on his clock.
A tray of spare cuckoos waiting for their clocks, beaks all pointing the same way, like a very small choir.
Nein, nein! Those are counted! Forty-seven cuckoos. If one goes missing, I will know. I will always know.
Forty-six cuckoos. She'll know. Eventually.
Vasko's clock, with an ordinary cuckoo inside. At noon tomorrow it will say "cuckoo", and absolutely nothing else will happen.
A grand clock on a stand, carved with pine leaves. And two wires, red and yellow, running from the cuckoo's little door down into the base. That's not a clock. That's a detonator with a pendulum.
Ah, the Colonel's clock! He brought his own cuckoo. Very heavy cuckoo. He says at noon tomorrow it must sing, "and open a door". A romantic, the Colonel.
At noon the cuckoo pops out, closes the circuit, and blows the ice door off Vasko's hangar. And out fly twelve aircraft.
Frau Zimmerli's workbench: tiny screwdrivers, springs, gears, and a lamp that has been on since 1946.
Frau Zimmerli, the clockmaker: spectacles on a chain, sawdust in her hair, and the patience of a woman who has built four thousand cuckoos by hand.
And this one, the Grand Alpine, has a cow that moos at six. Only one in the world. Look, look!
The clock on the wall, with Brunner's name on it. It's stopped.
Herr Brunner's! Forty years I have kept it for him, and every year he comes in and says: "Frau Zimmerli, never, never change the time on that clock." Eleven forty-five and thirty seconds.
I think it is the moment his bank was founded. Or the moment he fell in love. With a banker, you cannot tell the difference.
One, one, four, five, three, nought. Six digits. A Swiss vault takes six digits.
Frau Zimmerli, what's the very finest clock in the shop?
Oh! Oh, you must see the Grand Alpine, in the window. Come, come, it has a cow!
Look at this. A hundred and twelve parts. A cow that moos at six, a milkmaid at seven, and at eight, a very small avalanche.
She has her back to the tray of cuckoos. Now.
Look as long as you like. Everything ticks.
Please, do not touch the Colonel's clock! He was very particular. He threatened to shoot me. Very politely.
Vasko's heavy metal cuckoo out, Frau Zimmerli's wooden one in. At noon tomorrow it will pop out, say "cuckoo", and close nothing at all.
The Colonel's clock. For the hangar.
All ready, Herr Captain. Wound, oiled, and set for noon.
You. Ski instructor. Have we met?
Everybody's met a ski instructor, Captain. Knees!
...Hmph.
Nine hours on a ledge in the top station, waiting for the bank to open. The goose slept. I didn't. Brunner's vault, a door to Vasko's hangar, and two minutes to noon.
A vault door two metres across and a metre thick, with a card slot and a keypad beside it. Swiss engineering: nothing gets in, nothing gets out, and it's always on time.
The keypad is dark. It wants a card first.
Brunner's pass in the slot. The keypad lights up and asks, very politely, for six digits.
A keypad and a card slot. Six digits. The Swiss don't believe in four.
Dark. It wants Brunner's card first.
Rows of deposit boxes, and on a lectern in the middle, the ledger of numbered accounts. One of them has been paying for twelve aircraft.
A steel door into the hangar, and through its little window, twelve black aircraft in a row under a roof of blue ice. And at the far end, a door of solid ice, waiting for a cuckoo.
Locked from the other side. I can hear Vasko in there, whistling. Badly.
A steel desk with a lamp and a calendar. Tomorrow is ringed in red. Vasko's writing: "NOON. DOOR. CHAMPAGNE."
Six digits. The time on Brunner's clock, the one Frau Zimmerli must never change: eleven, forty-five, thirty.
Six digits. Brunner is the sort to hide his number in plain sight. Frau Zimmerli keeps a clock for him in the village.
Eleven, forty-five, thirty. Thank you, Herr Brunner, and thank you, Frau Zimmerli.
Numbered account 44-771. Deposits from London, every month for a year. Payments out to a Karvonian engineering company, eighty million francs. And the name of the account holder...
Noon.
Cuckoo!
Kolar... Why is the door not open?
The cuckoo is... a cuckoo, Colonel.
WHY IS THE CUCKOO A CUCKOO?
The account holder. Name: HARROW, JACK. Signature...
...mine. Well. A very good copy of mine.
Every payment for Nightglass, in my name, in a Swiss bank. Control didn't just frame me. He made me the buyer.
Brunner needs an instructor, and Sepp needs a man. I could be a man.
Herr Brunner is waiting for his lesson.
Brunner left something in the snowdrift.
The vault will want a number. Brunner's the sort to hide it in plain sight. Frau Zimmerli keeps a clock for him.
Vasko's clock is still in the shop, with its heavy metal cuckoo.
The valley station, and up to the glacier.
That grand clock in the middle of the shop: take a closer look.
Brunner's clock, on the wall by the window. What time does it say?
The clock with Brunner's name on it. Ask Frau Zimmerli about it.
I need a cuckoo from that tray while Frau Zimmerli is looking the other way. She's very proud of her clocks.
The spare cuckoo goes into Vasko's clock.
Back to the square.
The ledger, in the middle of the vault.
Brunner's pass in the slot, then the number from his clock.
Nothing special.
That won't work.
I don't think so.
Not a chance.
That doesn't help here.
Those two don't go together.
Don't look down. Don't look down. I looked down.
Colonel, if you're going to hold on to something, hold on to the cable, not my ear.
Harrow! The cable car is closed! Get off my cable!

Sixty metres, hand over hand, with a goose on his back. At the top, a locked door, a ledge out of the wind, and a long, cold night. The bank opens at half past eleven. Swiss banks are never late, not even inside a mountain.

In Monte Carlo, Jack beat Colonel Vasko at baccarat and won forty-one million francs. Vasko laughed. While they were playing, all twelve Nightglass aircraft had taken off. "I will see you in the mountains."

Franz has a friend at a bank. The friend has a cousin at another bank. The cousin says the money for Vasko's fleet went through Bank Brunner & Cie, whose vault is cut into a mountain above a village called Grindelhorn. Under the same glacier, the cousin says, is something that is not a bank.
Chalets, church bells, a cable car to the glacier, and a banker in a white ski suit shouting at a ski instructor.
A telex from Zürich, marked MOST SECRET: ACCOUNT 44-771, HOLDER HARROW J, EIGHTY MILLION FRANCS PAID TO VASKO. Control reads it, stirs his tea, and signs a warrant.
Twelve aircraft behind a door of ice that will not open. For now.
Cuckoo.
Chapter Ten: Burn Notice.
A steel card on a chain: BANK BRUNNER & CIE, GLETSCHERTRESOR. It opens the private cable car, and the vault at the top. It still has snow in the chain.
A little carved wooden cuckoo on a spring, from Frau Zimmerli's tray of forty-seven. It says "cuckoo" and nothing else. An honest bird.
Vasko's cuckoo: heavy, metal inside, with two wires in its tail. At noon it pops out, closes a circuit, and blows the ice door off Vasko's hangar. Now it just sits in my pocket, sulking.
Brunner's pass in the slot, a hum, and a little red cabin swings out over the valley with a ski instructor and a goose inside. A thousand metres of nothing underneath.

The cabin jerks to a stop. The lights go out. The loudspeaker crackles: "Good evening, ski instructor," says Captain Kolar. "Or should I say, Harrow. The cable car is closed for the night. Enjoy the view." Sixty metres of cable to the top station. It is a very long sixty metres.
